claim: More than 95% of crystal structures are determined at cryogenic temperatures (∼100 K) to reduce radiation damage.
source: However, more than 95% of crystal structures are determined at cryogenic temperatures (∼100 K) to reduce radiation damage by minimizing diffusion of reactive intermediates and chemical-damage-induced structural relaxations (Garman, 2010; Holton, 2009; Warkentin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garman, 2010; Holton, 2009; Warkentin et al., 2013

claim: Cryocooling can modify main chain and side chain conformational distributions throughout the protein, including at active sites and distal regions important for allosteric function.
source: Unfortunately, cryocooling can modify main chain and side chain conformational distributions throughout the protein, including at active sites and distal regions important for allosteric function (Fraser et al., 2011; Halle, 2004; Keedy, et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fraser et al., 2011; Halle, 2004; Keedy, et al., 2014

claim: Room temperature data collection reveals a multitude of previously 'hidden' alternative conformations that are not evident at cryogenic temperatures.
source: Recent studies have instead used room temperature data collection to reveal a multitude of previously 'hidden' alternative conformations that are not evident at cryogenic temperatures, many of which have important ramifications for determining molecular mechanisms (Deis et al., 2014; Fraser et al., 2009; Fukuda and Inoue, 2015; van den Bedem et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deis et al., 2014; Fraser et al., 2009; Fukuda and Inoue, 2015; van den Bedem et al., 2013

claim: A change in the character of conformational heterogeneity and/or protein dynamics occurs around 180–220 K.
source: Previous studies using a wide variety of biophysical probes including NMR, X-ray crystallography, and neutron scattering have revealed a change in the character of conformational heterogeneity and/or protein dynamics around 180–220 K (Doster, 2010; Frauenfelder et al., 2009; Lewandowski et al., 2015; Ringe and Petsko, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Doster, 2010; Frauenfelder et al., 2009; Lewandowski et al., 2015; Ringe and Petsko, 2003

claim: Eight high-resolution (1.34–1.58 Å) synchrotron crystallographic datasets of CypA were collected across temperatures from 100 to 310 K.
source: To probe the conformational landscape of CypA, we collected eight high-resolution (1.34 –1.58 Å) synchrotron crystallographic datasets across a wide range of temperatures from 100 to 310 K (Table 1) with no added cryoprotectants.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript with reference to Table 1

claim: The multitemperature synchrotron datasets of CypA were collected with no added cryoprotectants.
source: To probe the conformational landscape of CypA, we collected eight high-resolution (1.34 –1.58 Å) synchrotron crystallographic datasets across a wide range of temperatures from 100 to 310 K (Table 1) with no added cryoprotectants.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript

claim: For Ser99 and Leu98, mFo-DFc difference electron density maps are relatively featureless below 200 K, suggesting that a single conformation is valid below this temperature.
source: In the active-site network, the mFo-DFc difference electron density maps are relatively featureless below 200 K, suggesting that a single conformation is a valid fit below this temperature.
evidence: Based on analysis of electron density maps from the multitemperature datasets

claim: Positive and negative mFo-DFc peaks become gradually more prevalent as temperature increases above 200 K, suggesting that multiple conformations are increasingly required to explain the data.
source: By contrast, positive and negative mFo-DFc peaks become gradually more prevalent as temperature increases above 200 K, suggesting that multiple conformations are increasingly required to explain the data as temperature increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of electron density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: At 180 K and below, the active-site network of CypA is best modeled as a single state.
source: At 180 K and below, the active-site network is best modeled as a single state, with electron density corresponding to ordered water molecules clearly evident adjacent to Phe113 (Figure 2, top row).
evidence: Based on multiconformer models and electron density analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: At 240 K and above, multiple conformations in the active-site network of CypA provide a better explanation of the data.
source: At 240 K and above, by contrast, multiple conformations provide a better explanation of the data.
evidence: Based on multiconformer models and electron density analysis

claim: Met61 appears to populate additional conformations above 180 K.
source: Met61 appears to populate additional conformations above 180 K, although it is difficult to precisely define changes in its conformational ensemble as temperature increases.
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models across temperatures

claim: A 1.75 Å resolution radiation-damage-free XFEL dataset of CypA was collected at ambient temperature using serial femtosecond rotation crystallography.
source: To compare the distribution of alternative conformations between synchrotron and XFEL data, we collected two ambient-temperature datasets: a 1.75 Å resolution radiation-damage-free dataset using serial femtosecond rotation crystallography (Table 3) (Hirata et al., 2014; Schlichting, 2015; Suga et al., 2015)
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Table 3 and citations

claim: For the XFEL experiment, 1,239 individual diffraction images were collected from 71 crystals.
source: For the XFEL experiment, we collected 1,239 individual diffraction images, translating to unique unexposed regions of 71 crystals between each shot (Video 2), and processed them using cctbx.xfel (Hattne et al., 2014) with post-refinement in PRIME (Uervirojnangkoorn et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript with citations to processing methods

claim: The XFEL and synchrotron mFo-DFc difference maps reveal evidence for rate-limiting alternative conformations extending from the active site into the core of CypA.
source: In agreement with our previous room-temperature studies (Fraser et al., 2009), the XFEL and synchrotron mFo-DFc difference maps reveal evidence for the rate-limiting alternative conformations extending from the active site into the core of the protein (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Based on comparison of XFEL and synchrotron electron density maps shown in Figure 3A,B, with citation to previous work

claim: The backrub-coupled rotamer jump of Phe113 is apparent from a large positive mFo-DFc peak in both XFEL and synchrotron maps.
source: For example, the backrub-coupled (Davis et al., 2006) rotamer jump of Phe113 is apparent from a large positive mFo-DFc peak in both maps.
evidence: Based on analysis of electron density maps with citation to Davis et al., 2006

claim: Alternative conformations for core residue Ser99 are evident from mFo-DFc peaks and Ringer electron density sampling curves.
source: Alternative conformations for core residue Ser99 are also evident from mFo-DFc peaks (Figure 3A,B) and Ringer electron density sampling curves (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on analysis of electron density maps and Ringer curves shown in Figure 3

claim: XFEL crystallography provides a radiation-damage-free view of the functionally important alternative conformations of CypA.
source: The diffraction-before-destruction nature of XFEL experiments provides a radiation-damage-free view of the functionally important alternative conformations of CypA, confirming earlier synchrotron-based results.
evidence: Based on comparison of XFEL and synchrotron data

claim: The loop containing residues 79–83 exhibits conformational heterogeneity only at cryogenic temperatures.
source: For example, the loop containing residues 79–83 (Figure 4, Video 3) exhibits conformational heterogeneity only at cryogenic temperatures.
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models shown in Figure 4 and Video 3

claim: The loop containing residues 79–83 is well fit by a single conformation at 240 K and above.
source: This region is well fit by a single conformation at 240 K and above, but a secondary loop conformation is necessary to explain the electron density at 100, 150, and 180 K.
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models across temperatures

claim: The loop containing residues 79–83 requires a secondary conformation to explain the electron density at 100, 150, and 180 K.
source: This region is well fit by a single conformation at 240 K and above, but a secondary loop conformation is necessary to explain the electron density at 100, 150, and 180 K.
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models across temperatures

claim: The loop containing residues 79–83 is clearly single-state in the highest resolution (1.2 Å) dataset.
source: Additionally, the loop is clearly single-state in the highest resolution (1.2 Å) dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that the slightly lower resolution of the elevated-temperature datasets does not obscure a secondary conformation.
evidence: Based on analysis of the 1.2 Å dataset shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The secondary conformation of the 79–83 loop is accompanied by an ordered, partial-occupancy water molecule.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, the secondary conformation of the 79–83 loop is accompanied by an ordered, partial-occupancy water molecule (Figure 4, top row).
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models shown in Figure 4

claim: The observation of a secondary state for residues 79–83 at 100–180 K, but not at 240–310 K, suggests that it is enthalpically stabilized at lower temperatures.
source: The observation of a secondary state for residues 79–83 at 100–180 K, but not at 240–310 K, suggests that it is enthalpically stabilized at lower temperatures (Halle, 2004; Keedy et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational changes with citations to Halle, 2004; Keedy et al., 2014

claim: Curves of minor-state electron density versus temperature for Ser99 and Phe113 have a shallow slope at 180 K and below, but a much steeper slope at 240 K and above.
source: The resulting curves of minor-state electron density versus temperature have a shallow slope at 180 K and below, but a much steeper slope at 240 K and above (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of electron density shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: The electron density for the XFEL data is consistent with the data collection temperature (273 K) and the overall trends.
source: Additionally, the electron density for the XFEL data is consistent with the data collection temperature (273 K) and the overall trends.
evidence: Based on comparison of XFEL data with multitemperature synchrotron data

claim: A large change in χ1 bond order parameters for Phe113 occurs at 240 K and above.
source: Similar to the 2mFo-DFc electron density integration results for Phe113, we observed a large change in χ1 bond order parameters at 240 K and above (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on analysis of crystallographic order parameters shown in Figure 6A

claim: The average slope of conformational heterogeneity (1 – S2) versus temperature for the low-temperature fit lines (≤180 K) is 2.5 × 10–4 K–1.
source: The slopes of conformational heterogeneity (1 – S2) versus temperature were significantly different (p=1 × 10–62, paired T-test) on either side of this transition range: the average slope for the low-temperature fit lines (2.5 × 10–4 K–1) was an order of magnitude smaller than for the high-temperature fit lines (2.6 × 10–3 K–1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of order parameters across all residues

claim: The average slope of conformational heterogeneity (1 – S2) versus temperature for the high-temperature fit lines (≥240 K) is 2.6 × 10–3 K–1.
source: The slopes of conformational heterogeneity (1 – S2) versus temperature were significantly different (p=1 × 10–62, paired T-test) on either side of this transition range: the average slope for the low-temperature fit lines (2.5 × 10–4 K–1) was an order of magnitude smaller than for the high-temperature fit lines (2.6 × 10–3 K–1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of order parameters across all residues

claim: The slopes of conformational heterogeneity versus temperature are significantly different (p=1 × 10–62) on either side of the 180-240 K transition range.
source: The slopes of conformational heterogeneity (1 – S2) versus temperature were significantly different (p=1 × 10–62, paired T-test) on either side of this transition range: the average slope for the low-temperature fit lines (2.5 × 10–4 K–1) was an order of magnitude smaller than for the high-temperature fit lines (2.6 × 10–3 K–1).
evidence: Based on paired T-test statistical analysis

claim: The distribution of intersection temperatures for CypA residues is broad and asymmetrical, with an elongated tail from the peak near 250 K toward 200 K.
source: The distribution of these intersection temperatures is broad and asymmetrical, with an elongated tail from the peak near 250 K toward 200 K (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on analysis of intersection temperatures shown in Figure 6B

claim: CypA does not undergo a single global transition from having strongly temperature-dependent changes in side chain conformational heterogeneity to relatively temperature-independent behavior.
source: Our data suggest that CypA does not undergo a single global transition from having strongly temperature-dependent changes in side chain conformational heterogeneity to relatively temperature-independent behavior.
evidence: Based on analysis of the distribution of intersection temperatures across all residues

claim: Thermal depopulation of protein alternative conformations is sufficient to predict the existence of an average inflection without invoking a transition of the solvent.
source: Our observations are consistent with the idea that thermal depopulation of protein alternative conformations is sufficient to predict the existence of an average inflection without invoking a transition of the solvent.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data with predictions from high-temperature fits

claim: The low temperature of the predicted inflection (∼100 K) and the large separation in low-temperature disorder between experimental data and predictions from high temperature suggest that thermal depopulation of protein alternative conformations cannot by itself account for the observed ∼200 K transition.
source: However, the low temperature of the predicted inflection (∼100 K), as well as the large separation in low-temperature disorder between our experimental data (data points in Figure 6C) and predictions from high temperature (red line in Figure 6C), suggest that thermal depopulation of protein alternative conformations cannot by itself account for the observed ∼200 K transition.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data with predictions shown in Figure 6C

claim: Data collected at high temperatures (>260 K) cannot be reliably extrapolated to predict conformational heterogeneity at low temperatures.
source: This large separation also indicates that data collected at high temperatures (>260 K) cannot be reliably extrapolated to predict conformational heterogeneity at low temperatures.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data with predictions from high-temperature fits

claim: Data from low temperatures (≤180 K) cannot be simply extrapolated to predict the features of the energy landscape that may be important above ∼200 K.
source: It also follows that data from low temperatures (≤180 K) cannot be simply extrapolated to predict the features of the energy landscape that may be important above ∼200 K.
evidence: Based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity

claim: Roughly 67% of residues in CypA remain within one rotamer well across all temperatures.
source: Roughly 67% of residues (e.g. Phe8) remain within one rotamer well across all temperatures.
evidence: Based on decomposition of order parameters into B-factor versus discrete-conformers components

claim: Approximately 13% of residues in CypA populate clearly separable multiple rotameric states at high temperatures, and then show complete depopulation of minority states on cooling so that only a single rotameric state remains at 180 K and below.
source: Approximately 13% of residues (e.g. Ser99 and Phe113) populate clearly separable multiple rotameric states at high temperatures, and then show complete depopulation of minority states on cooling so that only a single rotameric state remains at 180 K and below.
evidence: Based on decomposition of order parameters into B-factor versus discrete-conformers components

claim: 6% of residues in CypA continue to populate multiple rotameric states at or below 180 K.
source: However, 6% of residues (e.g. Thr5) continue to populate multiple rotameric states at or below 180 K.
evidence: Based on decomposition of order parameters into B-factor versus discrete-conformers components

claim: An additional 6% of residues in CypA populate new rotameric states only at or below 180 K.
source: An additional 6% of residues (e.g. Lys91) populate new rotameric states only at or below 180 K.
evidence: Based on decomposition of order parameters into B-factor versus discrete-conformers components

claim: The active-site network of CypA appears subdivided based on the apparent intersection or transition temperatures of the constituent residues, with Ser99 and Phe113 behaving most similarly to each other.
source: However, using our new multitemperature data, this network appears subdivided based on the apparent intersection or transition temperatures of the constituent residues, with Ser99 and Phe113 behaving most similarly to each other (Figure 7, Video 4).
evidence: Based on analysis of intersection temperatures mapped to the structure shown in Figure 7

claim: The extensive heterogeneity in the temperature response of individual residues in CypA provides direct evidence for underlying energetic heterogeneity.
source: The extensive heterogeneity in the temperature response of individual residues in CypA that we observe here provides additional direct evidence for this underlying energetic heterogeneity.
evidence: Based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity across all residues

claim: No appreciable temperature evolution of individual conformer occupancies or B-factors occurs at 180 K and below in CypA.
source: Indeed, here we see no appreciable temperature evolution of individual conformer occupancies or B-factors at 180 K and below, and the average disorder at these temperatures is far in excess of what is predicted from high-temperature extrapolations.
evidence: Based on analysis of multiconformer models across temperatures

claim: The average disorder at 180 K and below in CypA is far in excess of what is predicted from high-temperature extrapolations.
source: Indeed, here we see no appreciable temperature evolution of individual conformer occupancies or B-factors at 180 K and below, and the average disorder at these temperatures is far in excess of what is predicted from high-temperature extrapolations.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data with predictions from high-temperature fits

claim: The persistence of multiple rotameric states at low temperatures in CypA is consistent with solvent arrest that impedes further changes in side chain disorder.
source: Moreover, the persistence of multiple rotameric states at low temperatures is consistent with solvent arrest that impedes further changes in side chain disorder.
evidence: Based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity

claim: Averaging over side chain disorder in all residues of CypA yields an apparent transition near 250 K.
source: Averaging over side chain disorder in all residues yields an apparent transition near 250 K (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Based on analysis of residue-averaged order parameters shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 7

claim: There is no evidence of tight cooperativity or of a collective global response near 250 K in CypA that would be expected in the case of a 'true' dynamical transition.
source: We find no evidence of tight cooperativity or of a collective global response near 250 K that would be expected in the case of a 'true' dynamical transition.
evidence: Based on analysis of the heterogeneous temperature dependence of individual side chains

claim: The data are consistent with local, non-cooperative freeze-out of conformational states defined by the energy landscape over a broad temperature range.
source: Instead, our data are consistent with local, non-cooperative freeze-out of conformational states defined by the energy landscape over a broad temperature range.
evidence: Based on analysis of the heterogeneous temperature dependence of individual side chains

claim: The heterogeneous response of side chain order parameters to temperature in CypA is driven largely by the changes to the populations of alternative conformations, which 'flat-line' at different temperatures across CypA.
source: The heterogeneous response of side chain order parameters to temperature is driven largely by the changes to the populations of alternative conformations, which 'flat-line' at different temperatures across CypA.
evidence: Based on analysis of order parameters and alternative conformations across temperatures

claim: The active-site network of CypA adopts two substates, which are primarily distinguished by Phe113 rotamer interconversion.
source: To bridge these views, we propose that the active-site network adopts two substates, which are primarily distinguished by Phe113 rotamer interconversion.
evidence: Proposed model based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity

claim: Each of the two substates of the CypA active-site network adopts a differently weighted ensemble of conformations for other residues.
source: Each of these substates adopts a differently weighted ensemble of conformations for other residues (Figure 8B).
evidence: Proposed model illustrated in Figure 8B

claim: Met61 and Arg55 can switch rotamers more easily than Ser99 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (p) rotamer pointed toward Ser99.
source: In this model, Met61 and Arg55 can switch rotamers more easily than Ser99 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (p) rotamer pointed toward Ser99, whereas Ser99 can switch rotamers more easily than Met61 and Arg55 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (m) rotamer pointed toward Met61.
evidence: Proposed model based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity

claim: Ser99 can switch rotamers more easily than Met61 and Arg55 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (m) rotamer pointed toward Met61.
source: In this model, Met61 and Arg55 can switch rotamers more easily than Ser99 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (p) rotamer pointed toward Ser99, whereas Ser99 can switch rotamers more easily than Met61 and Arg55 when Phe113 is in its χ1 gauche (m) rotamer pointed toward Met61.
evidence: Proposed model based on analysis of temperature-dependent conformational heterogeneity

claim: Phe113 has the lowest 'flat-lining' temperature of the active-site network.
source: This model is consistent with Phe113 having the lowest 'flat-lining' temperature of the network (Figure 7), and makes sense sterically because of the large size of the aromatic ring.
evidence: Based on analysis of intersection temperatures shown in Figure 7

claim: The proposed model for CypA active-site network dynamics is consistent with the timescales and temperature dependencies of motion assigned by solid-state NMR studies of crystalline protein GB1.
source: These hypothesized motions are consistent with the timescales and temperature dependencies of motion assigned by solid-state NMR studies of crystalline protein GB1 (Lewandowski et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with cited NMR study

claim: The proposed model helps explain the difficulty of fitting NMR relaxation data for perturbed versions of the active-site network as a single collective exchange process.
source: Furthermore, the model helps explain the difficulty of fitting NMR relaxation data for perturbed versions of the active-site network as a single collective exchange process (Schlegel et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison with cited NMR study

claim: The aromatic ring of Phe113 could play a dominant role in determining the chemical shift changes of the surrounding residues.
source: The aromatic ring of Phe113 could play a dominant role in determining the chemical shift changes of the surrounding residues.
evidence: Proposed explanation based on the model

claim: Wild-type CypA was produced and crystallized as previously reported by Fraser et al., 2009.
source: Wild-type CypA was produced and crystallized as previously reported (Fraser et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to previous work

claim: CypA crystals were grown by mixing equal volumes of well solution (100 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 23% PEG 3350, 5 mM TCEP) and protein (60 mg mL–1 in 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP) in the hanging-drop format.
source: Briefly, crystals were grown by mixing equal volumes of well solution (100 mM (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid) HEPES pH 7.5, 23% PEG 3350, 5 mM Tris (2-carboxymethyl) phosphine [TCEP]) and protein (60 mg mL –1 in 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP) in the hanging-drop format.
evidence: Directly stated experimental method

claim: Multitemperature synchrotron data were collected at CHESS beamline A1 with a 100 µm collimator using a wavelength of 0.9767 Å.
source: For the multitemperature synchrotron datasets at 100, 150, 180, 240, 260, 280, 300, and 310 K, we collected data at the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source (CHESS) at beamline A1 with a 100 µm collimator using a wavelength of 0.9767 Å.
evidence: Directly stated experimental method

claim: Crystals for multitemperature synchrotron data collection were stripped of excess mother liquor using NVH oil.
source: Crystals were looped by hand, stripped of excess mother liquor (100 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 23% PEG 3350, 5 mM TCEP) using NVH oil (Warkentin and Thorne, 2009), and placed directly into the nitrogen-gas cryostream pre-set to the desired temperature at the beamline.
evidence: Directly stated experimental method with citation

claim: Water inside protein crystals is nanoconfined so that ice nucleation is dramatically suppressed, but water outside crystallizes readily and rapidly.
source: Water inside protein crystals is nanoconfined so that ice nucleation is dramatically suppressed, but water outside crystallizes readily and rapidly.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about protein crystal behavior

claim: Careful removal of all excess solvent from the crystal surface is essential to obtaining ice-free diffraction between 260 K and 180 K without using large cryoprotectant concentrations.
source: Careful removal of all excess solvent from the crystal surface is essential to obtaining ice-free diffraction between 260 K and 180 K without using large cryoprotectant concentrations.
evidence: Statement based on experimental experience

claim: For the XFEL experiment, multiple diffraction images per crystal were collected using a 10-µm X-ray beam with each irradiation point separated by at least 25–40 µm to avoid collateral radiation damage.
source: For the XFEL experiment, we collected multiple diffraction images per crystal using a 10-µm X-ray beam with each irradiation point separated by at least 25–40 µm to avoid collateral radiation damage.
evidence: Directly stated experimental method

claim: A total of 1,239 still diffraction images were collected from 71 CypA crystals over the course of two experiments using a goniometer setup and a Rayonix MX325HE detector at LCLS-XPP.
source: A total of 1,239 still diffraction images were collected from 71 CypA crystals over the course of two experiments using a goniometer setup and a Rayonix MX325HE detector at LCLS-XPP (Cohen et al., 2014) (Video 2).
evidence: Directly stated experimental method with citation

claim: All XFEL data were collected at ambient temperature (approximately 273 K).
source: All data were collected at ambient temperature (approximately 273 K).
evidence: Directly stated experimental condition

claim: To prevent dehydration, crystals for XFEL data collection were coated with paratone oil immediately after looping.
source: To prevent dehydration, crystals were coated with paratone oil immediately after looping and mounted on the goniometer at the XPP endstation of LCLS using the SAM sample exchange robot (Cohen et al., 2002).
evidence: Directly stated experimental method with citation

claim: The synchrotron datasets were indexed, integrated, and scaled using XDS and XSCALE.
source: The synchrotron datasets were indexed, integrated, and scaled using XDS and XSCALE, and intensities were subsequently converted to structure factor amplitudes using XDSCONV.
evidence: Directly stated data processing method

claim: All multitemperature synchrotron datasets were from single crystals.
source: All datasets were from single crystals.
evidence: Directly stated experimental detail

claim: The XFEL data were processed using cctbx.xfel.
source: The XFEL data were processed using cctbx.xfel  (Hattne et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated data processing method with citation

claim: Of the 1,239 XFEL images collected, 772 were indexed and their intensities were integrated.
source: Of the 1,239 images collected, 772 were indexed and their intensities were integrated.
evidence: Directly stated data processing result

claim: Post-refinement for XFEL data was performed using PRIME.
source: Post-refinement, as implemented by PRIME  (post-refinement and merging, version date: November 11, 20:22:51 2014) (Uervirojnangkoorn et al., 2015), was used to correct the intensity measurements and merge the data.
evidence: Directly stated data processing method with citation

claim: Initial phases for each dataset were calculated by performing molecular replacement with phenix.auto_mr using PDB ID 2cpl as a search model.
source: For each dataset, we calculated initial phases by performing molecular replacement with phenix.auto_mr using PDB ID 2cpl as a search model.
evidence: Directly stated model building method

claim: A coupled side chain–backbone 'backrub' motion of −10° for Ser99 was necessary to match the Cα and Cβ positions of the minor conformation as modeled in PDB ID 3k0n.
source: A coupled side chain–backbone 'backrub' motion (Davis et al., 2006) of −10° for Ser99 (see Figure 5A) was necessary to match the Cα and Cβ positions of the minor conformation as modeled in PDB ID 3k0n; using this modified backbone indeed yielded maximal minor-conformation Ringer peaks for our multitemperature datasets.
evidence: Directly stated analysis method with citation

claim: No backrub motion was necessary for Leu98 due to the different type of backbone displacement.
source: No backrub motion was necessary for Leu98 due to the different type of backbone displacement (Fraser et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated analysis result with citation

claim: B-factor-influenced order parameters (S2) were calculated as previously reported by Fenwick et al., 2014.
source: We calculated B-factor-influenced order parameters (S2) as previously reported (Fenwick et al., 2014) except that we monitored one of two different types of bond vector.
evidence: Directly stated analysis method with citation

claim: All negative order parameters (caused by high B-factors) were floored to 0.
source: All negative order parameters (caused by high B-factors) were floored to 0.
evidence: Directly stated data processing step

claim: χ1 order parameters were floored for 7 residues in CypA.
source: χ1 order parameters were floored for 7 residues, and side chain-end order parameters were floored for 23 residues.
evidence: Directly stated data processing result

claim: Side chain-end order parameters were floored for 23 residues in CypA.
source: χ1 order parameters were floored for 7 residues, and side chain-end order parameters were floored for 23 residues.
evidence: Directly stated data processing result
